passage: When Jyoti, her aunt, came down the lane from the bus stand, two-year-old Ankita spotted her from the doorstep. She squealed, waved both arms and ran with wobbly steps. Then a man from the next village stopped to ask directions. Ankita stared at him for a long moment, gripped her mother's dupatta and turned her face away. When he left she went back to her toys as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: Where was Ankita when she saw Jyoti?
qa.a: She was on the doorstep of her home.

qa.q: What was Ankita likely feeling toward Jyoti versus the stranger, and what else might explain her behaviour with the man?
qa.a: She seems happy and excited with Jyoti, and unsure with the man, since she stared and turned away. She could also have been startled by his sudden arrival.

qa.q: How could Ankita's mother respond to the staring?
qa.a: She can stay close, speak calmly to the man, and let Ankita watch without pushing her to greet him. 🙂

qa.q: How might the man feel about being turned away from?
qa.a: He may feel a bit awkward, but a warm word from her mother can help him see it as ordinary toddler caution.

grounding: A toddler shows recognition with excited sounds and reaching, and stares or turns away around strangers.

passage: The doorbell rang in the Lisbon flat. Paulo, one and a half, was on the rug when Soo-ah, his childminder, came in. He squealed and crawled toward her, reaching up. A minute later a plumber walked in behind her. Paulo went silent, stared at the man's cap and turned to bury his face in Soo-ah's leg. She rubbed his back. "He is new to you, Paulo."

qa.q: Who arrived first at the door?
qa.a: Soo-ah, the childminder, arrived first.

qa.q: What might Paulo be feeling about the plumber, and what other explanation could there be?
qa.a: He is probably feeling wary of an unfamiliar face, since he stared and hid. He might also have been surprised by the cap.

qa.q: What could Soo-ah do next to help Paulo?
qa.a: She can keep him close, let the plumber speak softly from a distance, and give Paulo time to look before he is asked to engage. 🙂

qa.q: How might the plumber feel about the baby's silence?
qa.a: He might feel unsure whether he is welcome, but seeing Soo-ah stay calm can show him it is only newness.

grounding: A toddler shows recognition of a familiar person with squeals and reaching, and stares or turns away from a stranger.

passage: I'm Arnab. I deliver milk in the colony, and little Parveen waits for me every morning at her gate. When she sees my bicycle, she squeals, bounces and reaches for the bell. Last week I was ill, and another man took my round. Her mother told me Parveen stood at the gate and just stared at him, very still, then turned and walked back inside. When I came back on Monday, she squealed again.

qa.q: What does Parveen reach for when she sees Arnab?
qa.a: The bell on the bicycle.

qa.q: What might Parveen have been feeling when the other man came?
qa.a: She was probably confused and wary with a stranger in Arnab's place, staring and turning away; her squeal on Monday shows joy at seeing Arnab again.

qa.q: What could the new delivery man do if he has to cover the round again?
qa.a: Keep a friendly distance and let Parveen watch him, without expecting her to greet him.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel being greeted with a squeal?
qa.a: Arnab likely feels pleased and touched to be recognised and missed.

grounding: A milk deliverer notices a toddler greet him with delight and stare and turn away from a stranger in his place.

passage:
Nani arrived from Kolkata on Saturday. Tarun stared at her from Ammi's lap and turned his face away when she smiled.
Tuesday: he sat on the kitchen floor and watched Rehana Nani roll rotis, very serious.
The next Saturday: Rehana came in from the market. Tarun squealed, bounced on his toes and reached up both arms. "Na-na!"

qa.q: Where did Nani arrive from?
qa.a: From Kolkata.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he turned his face away on Saturday?
qa.a: He didn't yet recognise her and felt wary of a new face.

qa.q: What helped Tarun come to know his Nani?
qa.a: Time, and being able to watch her do everyday things like rolling rotis without pressure.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel the next Saturday?
qa.a: She would likely feel delighted and moved that Tarun now recognised and welcomed her. 🤍

grounding: Over a week a toddler moves from staring and turning away from his grandmother to recognising her with delight.

passage:
Maria had been away in Kuwait for eight months. When she walked into the Panaji flat, Elizabeth stared at her from her mother's arms. Then Maria said, "Hello, my Lizzie," in her old sing-song. Elizabeth's face burst into a smile, and she lunged toward her, arms out.
Behind Maria came her new husband. Elizabeth took one look at him and stared, still, then turned her face into Maria's neck.

qa.q: How long had Maria been away?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What made Elizabeth recognise Maria?
qa.a: Hearing Maria's old sing-song voice; Elizabeth felt joyful and lunged toward her, arms out.

qa.q: What could Maria's husband do to help Elizabeth get to know him?
qa.a: Give her time and keep a gentle distance, letting her watch him until she feels ready.

qa.q: How might Maria's husband feel when Elizabeth turns away?
qa.a: He might feel a little left out, but understand that he is still a stranger to her.

grounding: A toddler recognises a returning family member's voice with delight and stares and turns away from a new person.

passage:
“Look who's here, Charu!” said Rekha as Nani came through the gate.
Charu squealed, bounced on Rekha's hip and stretched both arms out. “Na-na!”
Nani laughed and took her.
At the wedding that evening, Rekha's cousin from Pune bent close. “Hello, Charu! Remember me?”
Charu stared at him, very still, then turned her face into Rekha's shoulder.
“She doesn't remember me?” he said.
“She was a tiny baby last time,” said Rekha.

qa.q: What did Charu say when she saw Nani?
qa.a: Charu said "Na-na!"

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she saw Nani, and how was that different with the cousin?
qa.a: With Nani she was delighted and eager, shown by her squeal and outstretched arms; with the cousin she stared and turned away because he felt like a stranger and she was unsure.

qa.q: How could the cousin help Charu get to know him?
qa.a: He could give her time and distance, talk with Rekha nearby, and let Charu look at him before expecting a greeting.

qa.q: How did Rekha's cousin feel when Charu turned away?
qa.a: He seemed a little hurt and surprised that she did not remember him.

grounding: It shows a toddler recognising a familiar person with a squeal and reaching, and staring and turning away from someone who feels like a stranger.
